metadata.section: Chapter 6: THE BREEDER'S EQUATION FRAMED WITHIN THE PRICE EQUATION
subsections: Partial Covariance and the Spurious Response to Selection
metadata.source_title: Evolution and Selection of Quantitative Traits

blocks.content: There are two ways to generate a nonzero $ \sigma(w, \overline{z} \parallel z) $. First, both regressions $ (w_i \text{ on } z_i \text{ and } \overline{z}_i \text{ on } z_i) $ may be nonlinear, and, as a result, their residuals may be correlated, generating a spurious response (e.g., Figure 6.5). Second, even if one (or both) of these regressions is linear, if both $ w_i $ and $ \overline{z}_i $ are correlated through an unmeasured variable (such as an environmental effect), their residuals, after being regressed on $ z_{i} $, can still be correlated, again generating a potentially spurious response (Chapter 20 examines this process in more detail).

Example 6.8. One can imagine several measures of the residual dependency between two variables (say x and y) once the effects of a third (z) is removed. One is conditional covariance, $ \sigma(x, y \mid z) $, defined as the covariance conditioned on the value of z: [[SEE_FORMULA:6.33a]]

Heywood’s decomposition uses an alternative measure of dependency, the partial covariance [[SEE_FORMULA:6.33b]] where $ e_x $ and $ e_y $ are the residuals for the linear regression of $ x $ on $ z $ and of $ y $ on $ z $. We use the notation $ \|z $ in place of $ |z $ to distinguish between partial and conditional covariances. If the three variables are multivariate normal, the conditional and partial covariances are equal, but generally they differ (Lawrance 1976; Baba et al. 2006).

The partial covariance can be expressed in terms of the various pairwise covariances between the three variables, as follows. The linear regression of x on z can be written as [[SEE_FORMULA:6.33c]] with a similar expression for $ e_{y} $. Substituting these into Equation 6.33b and ignoring the mean terms (which, as constants, do not factor in the covariance) yields [[SEE_FORMULA:6.33d]]
The last term can be expressed as either $ \beta_{x|z}\sigma(y,z) $ or $ \beta_{y|z}\sigma(x,z) $. Applying Equation 6.33d by taking $ x = w $ and $ y = \overline{z} $ yields [[SEE_FORMULA:6.33e]]
Rearranging this last expression yields [[SEE_FORMULA:6.33f]] which is used to obtain Equation 6.32.
